segments.speaker: Host A
segments.text: Welcome back to the show. Today we're talking about how small towns rebuild their main streets.

segments.speaker: Host A
segments.text: Our guest has spent ten years studying it. Thanks for coming on.

segments.speaker: Guest B
segments.text: Thanks for having me. It's a topic I care about a lot.

segments.speaker: Host A
segments.text: Before we start, this episode is brought to you by Acme Mattresses. Use code SLEEP for ten percent off.

segments.speaker: Guest B
segments.text: So the first thing people get wrong is thinking it starts with money. It starts with foot traffic.

segments.speaker: Guest B
segments.text: If nobody walks past a shop, no grant will save it. Towns that widened sidewalks saw rents recover first.

segments.speaker: Host A
segments.text: That's surprising. Why sidewalks and not parking?

segments.speaker: Guest B
segments.text: Parking brings cars, not people who linger. Lingering is what fills cafes and bookshops.

takeaways.text: Main streets recover when foot traffic returns; wider sidewalks did more than parking.

segments.speaker: Host A
segments.text: Let's talk about the downside. Who loses when a main street gets popular again?

segments.speaker: Guest B
segments.text: Long-time tenants, usually. Rents rise and the hardware store becomes a wine bar.

segments.speaker: Guest B
segments.text: Some towns cap commercial rent increases for existing tenants. It's controversial but it works.

segments.speaker: Host A
segments.text: That's all for today. Thanks for listening.
